What exactly is the Pentose Phosphate Pathway?

blocks.x: The Pentose Phosphate Pathway (PPP) — also known as the Hexose Monophosphate Shunt or the Phosphogluconate Pathway — is a "side branch" off glucose metabolism. Unlike glycolysis, which is mainly about energy, the PPP has two very different jobs: making pentose sugars (5-carbon sugars) for building nucleotides and nucleic acids (DNA, RNA), and generating NADPH, a "reducing power" currency used for biosynthesis and antioxidant defense. It runs entirely in the cytosol.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — the recharge-and-repair shop next to the main factory

blocks.x: Think of glycolysis as the main assembly line, churning out energy. Right next door sits a smaller specialist shop — the PPP — that does two things the main line doesn't: it charges up rechargeable "batteries" (NADPH) that other departments borrow to build things or clean up mess, and it produces small spare parts (pentose sugars) used specifically for building genetic material. It can also recycle 3-, 4-, 6-, and 7-carbon sugars back and forth as needed, acting like a flexible parts-recycling counter.

The pathway runs in two phases: an oxidative phase (irreversible, generates NADPH) and a non-oxidative phase (reversible, interconverts sugars and can generate pentose sugars without spending any NADPH at all).

One thing that is easy to miss: the PPP produces no ATP, and consumes none either. It is not an energy pathway at all — its entire purpose is reducing power and building blocks. That is the cleanest way to separate it from glycolysis in an exam answer.

sections.title: Which tissues rely on this the most, and why?

blocks.x: NADPH from the PPP is mainly used for reductive biosynthesis — building fatty acids and steroids — and for defense against oxidative damage, especially via reduced glutathione.

c: Fatty acid synthesis (for breast milk fat)
Supplies NADPH for the NADPH oxidase respiratory burst that kills engulfed bacteria — if NADPH oxidase itself is faulty the result is chronic granulomatous disease, with recurrent infections
NADPH for cytochrome P450 drug and toxin detoxification

blocks.x: Red blood cells have no mitochondria at all — so unlike most cells, they can't make NADPH any other way. The PPP is their only source of NADPH, and that NADPH is what keeps their antioxidant defenses charged. This single fact explains almost everything about the clinical disorder covered later in this guide.

blocks.cap: Two NADPH banked, one CO₂ released, one 5-carbon sugar delivered — all in three steps.

blocks.x: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) oxidizes glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconolactone, reducing NADP⁺ to NADPH. This is the committed, rate-limiting step of the entire pathway.

6-Phosphogluconolactonase (also called lactonase) adds a molecule of water to 6-phosphogluconolactone, opening its ring to form 6-phosphogluconate. The enzyme requires Mg²⁺. The lactone ring is unstable and would open on its own eventually, but the enzyme makes it happen fast enough to be useful — and prevents the reactive lactone from lingering and damaging the cell. Exam trap: this middle step is a hydrolysis, not an oxidation — it produces no NADPH and releases no CO₂. Both NADPH molecules come from steps 1 and 3; the CO₂ comes only from step 3. If a question asks which step of the oxidative phase yields no reducing power, this is it.
6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase oxidizes 6-phosphogluconate while removing a carbon as CO₂, forming ribulose-5-phosphate and generating the 2nd NADPH.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a two-stop battery-charging counter

blocks.x: Picture a small counter with two charging docks in a row. Your glucose-6-phosphate "device" gets docked twice — once at G6PD, once at 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase — and each dock tops up one NADPH battery. Along the way, a bit of packaging (a carbon, as CO₂) is discarded, and what's handed back to you at the end is a smaller, 5-carbon spare part: ribulose-5-phosphate.

sections.title: A flexible recycling counter, tuned to what the cell actually needs

blocks.x: Unlike the oxidative phase, the non-oxidative phase is entirely reversible and doesn't touch NADPH at all. Its job is to interconvert 3-, 4-, 5-, 6-, and 7-carbon sugars, letting the cell dial the pathway's output toward whatever it needs most that day.

items.title: Step 1 — Two directions out of ribulose-5-phosphate

blocks.x: Phosphopentose isomerase converts ribulose-5-phosphate into ribose-5-phosphate — the building block used directly for nucleotide and nucleic acid synthesis. Alternatively, phosphopentose epimerase converts it into xylulose-5-phosphate, which feeds into further sugar rearrangements.

items.title: Step 2 — Transketolase & Transaldolase rearrange the rest

blocks.x: Transketolase — which needs thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the active form of vitamin B₁, plus Mg²⁺ — transfers 2-carbon units between sugars, while transaldolase (which needs no cofactor) transfers 3-carbon units. Working together, three 5-carbon pentose phosphates can be rearranged into two fructose-6-phosphate molecules and one glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate — both of which feed directly back into glycolysis.
The actual sequence, reaction by reaction

The summary above is what you quote in one line. This is what is really happening underneath — and it is where sedoheptulose-7-phosphate, the pathway’s famous 7-carbon sugar, appears. Start with three ribulose-5-phosphate molecules coming out of the oxidative phase.

blocks.title: Set up the substrates — isomerase and epimerase

blocks.x: Of the three ribulose-5-phosphates: one is isomerised to ribose-5-phosphate (C5) by phosphopentose isomerase, and two are epimerised to xylulose-5-phosphate (C5) by phosphopentose epimerase. You now hold: 1 × ribose-5-P and 2 × xylulose-5-P.

Xylulose-5-P (C5) + Ribose-5-P (C5) → Sedoheptulose-7-phosphate (C7) + Glyceraldehyde-3-P (C3) Transketolase lifts a 2-carbon unit off xylulose-5-phosphate and hands it to ribose-5-phosphate. The donor shrinks from 5 to 3 carbons (becoming GAP); the acceptor grows from 5 to 7 carbons (becoming sedoheptulose-7-phosphate). Check the carbons: 5 + 5 = 7 + 3. Nothing is lost — the pathway is only reshuffling.

Sedoheptulose-7-P (C7) + Glyceraldehyde-3-P (C3) → Erythrose-4-phosphate (C4) + Fructose-6-P (C6) Transaldolase moves a 3-carbon unit from sedoheptulose-7-phosphate onto the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate made in step B. The C7 donor drops to C4 (erythrose-4-phosphate); the C3 acceptor rises to C6 — your first fructose-6-phosphate. Check the carbons: 7 + 3 = 4 + 6. Transaldolase needs no cofactor — a favourite one-mark question.

Xylulose-5-P (C5) + Erythrose-4-P (C4) → Fructose-6-P (C6) + Glyceraldehyde-3-P (C3) The second xylulose-5-phosphate now donates another 2-carbon unit, this time to erythrose-4-phosphate. That gives your second fructose-6-phosphate, and the leftover donor becomes glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. Check the carbons: 5 + 4 = 6 + 3. Note that transketolase is used twice and transaldolase only once.

blocks.title: The bookkeeping — why it must balance

blocks.x: Three pentose phosphates go in: 3 × C5 = 15 carbons. What comes out is two fructose-6-phosphates and one glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate: (2 × 6) + 3 = 15 carbons. Not a single carbon is gained or lost in the whole non-oxidative phase — unlike the oxidative phase, which loses one carbon per glucose as CO₂. If your carbons don’t balance in an exam answer, you have dropped a step.

• Transketolase moves 2, transaldolase moves 3 — “keTOlase” for two. • The carbon story runs 5+5 → 7+3, then 7+3 → 4+6, then 5+4 → 6+3. • Only transketolase needs a vitamin (B₁, as TPP). Transaldolase needs nothing. • Sedoheptulose (C7) and erythrose-4-P (C4) exist only as hand-over intermediates — they are never end products.
Putting the whole pathway together, three glucose-6-phosphates entering the oxidative phase and passing through the non-oxidative phase give:
3 Glucose-6-P + 6 NADP⁺ → 2 Fructose-6-P + 1 Glyceraldehyde-3-P + 3 CO₂ + 6 NADPH + 6 H⁺

Clinical hook worth remembering: because transketolase depends on thiamine, its activity in red blood cells is used as a laboratory test for thiamine (vitamin B₁) deficiency — the deficiency behind beriberi and Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Erythrose-4-phosphate is also the link into the shikimate pathway in plants and microbes, which is why humans must take in aromatic amino acids from the diet.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a currency exchange that adapts to what you actually need

blocks.x: Most pathways are like a one-way production line. The non-oxidative phase is more like a flexible currency exchange counter that can run in whichever direction the customer needs:

c: Oxidative phase runs fully; excess ribulose-5-P is converted back into glycolytic intermediates (fructose-6-P, GAP) by the non-oxidative phase.
The oxidative phase's ribulose-5-P output is used directly for nucleotide synthesis — little further conversion needed.
The non-oxidative phase runs in reverse, starting from glycolytic intermediates — producing pentose sugars without ever running the oxidative phase, so no NADPH is spent.
Both NADPH and ATP, very little ribose-5-P
Ribulose-5-P is converted all the way through to pyruvate, feeding both glycolysis and the Krebs cycle for additional ATP.

blocks.x: This is what makes the PPP so different from glycolysis: it isn't locked into one fixed direction. A rapidly dividing cell needing lots of DNA precursors can lean on ribose-5-phosphate production without necessarily needing much NADPH; a fat-storing cell needing lots of NADPH for lipid synthesis can lean the other way — and the same enzymes handle both scenarios.

sections.title: What controls the speed of the pathway?

blocks.x: G6PD — the very first enzyme — is the committed, rate-limiting step of the whole pathway, and it's controlled by something refreshingly simple: the availability of its substrate, NADP⁺.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a charging station that only ramps up when there's demand

blocks.x: Picture a phone-charging kiosk that only gets busy when a big pile of drained batteries (NADP⁺) shows up waiting to be recharged. When cells actively spend NADPH — powering fatty acid synthesis, neutralizing ROS — that spent NADPH becomes NADP⁺, and a high NADP⁺ concentration directly stimulates the PPP to replenish the supply. As soon as demand slows and NADP⁺ stops piling up, the pathway automatically slows down too — no separate "off switch" enzyme required. The non-oxidative phase, meanwhile, is controlled simply by the availability of its various sugar substrates.

There is also a slower, hormonal layer on top of this. In the well-fed state insulin increases the synthesis of G6PD (along with the other enzymes of fatty acid synthesis), so a body that is being fed and is building fat gradually raises its capacity to make NADPH. Think of NADP⁺ as the minute-to-minute accelerator, and insulin as the decision to install a bigger engine.

sections.title: What happens when the very first enzyme is faulty?

blocks.x: G6PD deficiency is one of the most common enzyme abnormalities in humans — affecting over 400 million people worldwide, with roughly 20% of the population in some parts of Africa carrying it.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a power station that only supplies one customer

blocks.x: Remember: red blood cells have no mitochondria, so the PPP is their only power station for NADPH. If G6PD is faulty, that power station's output drops — and because RBCs have no backup generator, they're hit hardest of any cell type in the body. Reduced NADPH means reduced glutathione regeneration, which can trigger acute hemolytic anemia — the destruction of red blood cells.

sections.title: What is glutathione, and why does it matter here?

blocks.x: <term d="A tripeptide made of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine; a potent cellular antioxidant that neutralizes reactive oxygen species.">Glutathione (GSH)</term> is a small tripeptide — built from glutamate, cysteine, and glycine — that acts as a powerful antioxidant, degrading <term d="Highly reactive, oxygen-containing molecules (like hydrogen peroxide) that can damage cell components if not neutralized.">reactive oxygen species (ROS)</term> that constantly arise in the oxygen-rich environment inside red blood cells.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — rust-proofing a metal gate

blocks.x: Oxygen is essential for RBCs to do their job, but it also constantly generates small amounts of reactive byproducts (ROS) — a bit like how exposure to air and moisture slowly rusts an iron gate. ROS attack the double bonds in the fatty molecules of the cell membrane, weakening it. Left unchecked, this membrane damage causes hemolysis — the cell rupturing. Glutathione is the "rust-proofing coat" that neutralizes ROS before they can do that damage.

Mature RBCs are totally dependent on NADPH from the PPP to regenerate glutathione from its oxidized form (GSSG) back to its active, reduced form (GSH), via the enzyme glutathione reductase. Reduced glutathione then detoxifies peroxides directly:
2 GSH + H₂O₂ → GSSG + 2 H₂O — glutathione "absorbs" the damaging hydrogen peroxide and converts it into harmless water. This step is catalysed by glutathione peroxidase, a selenium-dependent enzyme.
Learn it as a two-enzyme cycle — exams almost always test the pair together:

items: Glutathione peroxidase — spends GSH to destroy H₂O₂ (2 GSH → GSSG). Requires selenium.
Glutathione reductase — restores GSH from GSSG, and this is the step that consumes NADPH. Requires FAD, from vitamin B₂.

blocks.x: So the PPP never fights oxidative damage directly — it supplies the NADPH that keeps this cycle turning. Cut off the NADPH and the cycle stalls, leaving glutathione stuck in its useless oxidised form (GSSG). That is exactly what happens in G6PD deficiency.
Glutathione levels can be run down by stress, poor nutrition, environmental toxins, and simply ageing — and cells with low GSH become more susceptible to hemolysis.

Interestingly, carriers of G6PD-deficiency mutations have shown increased resistance to malaria — which is exactly why the condition is most common in tropical Africa, Asia, the Middle East, the Mediterranean, and Papua New Guinea — regions that historically carried heavy malaria burdens. It's the same kind of evolutionary trade-off seen with the sickle cell trait: a genetic quirk that causes problems under certain stress, but offers real protection against a historically bigger threat.

sections.title: Usually silent — until something sets it off

blocks.x: Most people with G6PD deficiency are completely asymptomatic day to day. The trouble starts when they're exposed to certain oxidative stressors — things that create a sudden surge of ROS the cell can't keep up with.

G6PD deficiency is X-linked recessive. That means males (who carry a single X chromosome) are affected far more often, while females are usually carriers — though a female can be affected if both X chromosomes carry the fault, and carriers can show mild effects because of random X-inactivation.

During an attack, haemoglobin is oxidised and clumps inside the red cell, forming Heinz bodies. The spleen then bites these clumps out of the cell, leaving the classic bite cells seen under the microscope.

G6PD A⁻ — common in Africa, the enzyme is unstable so only older red cells are lost; episodes are milder and self-limiting. G6PD Mediterranean — enzyme activity is far lower, so attacks are more severe and favism is typical. Neonatal jaundice is also a recognised presentation.

Bacterial and viral infections (the commonest trigger of all); certain painkillers and fever-reducers (aspirin, ibuprofen/NSAIDs); antimalarials (primaquine, chloroquine); antibiotics such as sulfonamides, dapsone and nitrofurantoin; naphthalene (household "mothballs" or "camphor balls"); and fava beans — eating them triggers the reaction known as favism — plus soybeans and some other legumes.

Paleness (especially in the mouth, lips, or tongue), extreme tiredness, rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, dizziness, jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes — especially concerning in newborns), and dark, tea-colored urine.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a small generator that copes fine until overloaded

blocks.x: Think of G6PD deficiency like owning a small backup generator that handles everyday household load just fine — until someone plugs in something large and unexpected all at once. Under normal daily conditions, a person can go their whole life without noticing anything. But a sudden oxidative "power surge" — an infection, the wrong medication, mothball fumes, or fava beans — can overload the RBC's limited antioxidant capacity within hours, triggering a burst of hemolysis.

sections.title: Special risks, and how the condition is managed

blocks.x: G6PD deficiency can contribute to poor pregnancy outcomes, including an increased risk of anaemia in pregnancy, spontaneous abortion, low birth-weight infants, and jaundice in the newborn.

The main strategy is simply avoiding known oxidative stressors. Beyond that: folic acid and iron supplements are useful; oxygen therapy may be required in some cases; and a blood transfusion may be needed if anaemia becomes severe. Hemolytic episodes are usually short-term, but can occasionally be life-threatening — so prompt recognition matters.

sections.title: Key takeaways

items: The PPP yields no ATP — it is a pathway for reducing power and building blocks, not for energy.
NADPH protects the cell through the glutathione cycle: glutathione peroxidase (selenium-dependent) spends GSH to destroy H₂O₂, and glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate it.
The Pentose Phosphate Pathway runs in the cytosol and produces both pentose sugars (for nucleotides/nucleic acids) and NADPH (for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense).
The oxidative phase is irreversible: 3 steps, 2 NADPH generated, 1 CO₂ released, ending in ribulose-5-phosphate. G6PD is the rate-limiting, committed step.
The non-oxidative phase is reversible and highly flexible — it can run in either direction depending on whether the cell needs more NADPH, more ribose-5-phosphate, or both.

The middle step of the oxidative phase (6-phosphogluconolactonase) is a hydrolysis — it yields no NADPH and no CO₂. Both NADPH come from G6PD and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase; the CO₂ comes only from the latter.
Regulation is driven mainly by NADP⁺ availability — high NADP⁺ (meaning NADPH has been spent) stimulates the pathway — with insulin raising G6PD levels over the longer term.
G6PD deficiency is X-linked recessive, so males are mainly affected; the blood film shows Heinz bodies and bite cells.
G6PD deficiency is extremely common, especially in malaria-endemic regions, due to an evolutionary trade-off offering malaria resistance.
Because RBCs lack mitochondria, they depend entirely on PPP-derived NADPH to regenerate glutathione, their main antioxidant defense.
Deficiency is usually silent until an oxidative stressor (infections, certain drugs, mothballs, fava beans) triggers acute hemolytic anemia.
Management centers on avoiding triggers, with supportive care (folic acid, iron, oxygen, transfusion) for acute episodes.

items.d: Glucose-6-P → 6-phosphogluconolactone. Produces 1st NADPH. Committed, irreversible step.
Non-oxidative phase: shuffles 3-7 carbon sugars around, no NADPH involved, fully reversible.
Depending on cell needs, the pathway can favor NADPH production, ribose-5-P for nucleotides, or feed back into glycolysis.
